speaker: Cliff Asness
title: Cliff Asness on Factor Investing and the History of Financial Economics
question: In institutional investing, how do private equity valuation practices distort the economics of comparing private funds to public markets?
guest: You can mark any asset at where you could sell it today, which for public markets is quite easy—you look up the price. The other end of the spectrum is marking it at what you think it's worth. My sense is private funds are mostly marking to their model, to what they think the thing is worth. What I object to is mixing different standards on an efficient frontier, using market prices for public assets and model prices for private assets—showing public equities at 16% volatility and private assets at 5% volatility. That's apples to oranges. Their true risk is much higher than reported; if we go through a ten-year bear market, that risk will show up. It can even matter for prospective returns going forward. Historically, you got paid a premium for owning an illiquid private asset because who wants something hard to sell? Today, many investors have grown to value smoothed marks because they're easier to stick with during market drawdowns. When not marking to market becomes a desired feature rather than a bug, investors pay up for it and accept lower expected returns going forward.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Private equity valuations distort the comparison mainly because fund assets are appraised infrequently by the managers themselves rather than priced continuously by a market. These quarterly, lagged, judgment-based marks smooth returns, which mechanically understates volatility, beta, and correlation with public equities. The result is what AQR's Cliff Asness calls "volatility laundering": leveraged companies that are economically riskier than public stocks appear safer, inflating Sharpe ratios and manufacturing apparent diversification. Studies that unsmooth the returns typically find betas well above 1, not the 0.5 or so that reported figures imply.

This feeds through to allocation models, which over-allocate to private assets because the inputs flatter them. Performance metrics add to the problem. IRRs are sensitive to cash-flow timing and can be boosted by subscription credit lines. They also assume reinvestment at the same rate, so they are not comparable to time-weighted public returns. Interim net asset values can be marked optimistically during fundraising, and they often lag public downturns, as in 2022.

Fairer comparisons use public market equivalent (PME) methods and benchmarks adjusted for leverage, size and sector, under which the net-of-fee outperformance shrinks substantially.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Private equity funds value illiquid holdings quarterly using appraisal models and selected comparables rather than continuous market-clearing prices. This lagged, discretionary process smooths reported returns, creating what critics call "volatility laundering." Because marks adjust slowly during downturns, private funds display artificially low volatility, muted drawdowns, and understated beta and correlation to public equities. Risk-adjusted metrics like Sharpe ratios and alpha are consequently inflated, leading institutional asset-allocation models to overweight private markets while underpricing their underlying leverage, equity, and illiquidity risks.

Valuation practices also skew direct return comparisons. Headline metrics such as internal rate of return (IRR) and valuation multiples blend realized cash distributions with manager-estimated net asset values of unsold companies, allowing optimistic interim marks to prop up reported performance during fundraising or stalled exit environments—a gap exposed when secondary stakes trade at steep discounts to stated NAV. Comparing these appraisal-dependent, money-weighted IRRs (often further boosted by subscription credit lines) against mark-to-market, time-weighted public indices creates an apples-to-oranges distortion that systematically flatters private funds relative to liquid public equivalents.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Private equity is valued by appraisal, usually quarterly and with a lag. Managers mark holdings using models and comparables, not market prices. This smooths reported returns. Measured volatility and correlation with stocks come out far lower than the true economic risk. Cliff Asness calls this "volatility laundering." The result is inflated Sharpe ratios, and allocation models that treat private equity as a diversifier when it is really a leveraged, illiquid bet on small and mid-sized companies.

Timing makes it worse. In 2022, public equities fell about 18% while many buyout funds barely cut their marks. Investors looked overweight public assets (the "denominator effect"), and private equity's relative performance looked better than it was.

The return metrics add more problems. IRR is money-weighted and depends on timing. Subscription credit lines, quick partial exits and NAV loans can raise it without creating value. Interim IRRs also depend on unrealized marks that the manager sets.

Fair comparisons should use realized cash flows and public market equivalent (PME) methods. The benchmark should be leverage- and size-matched (small-cap value rather than the S&P 500) and should count all fees. On that basis, much of the apparent outperformance shrinks or disappears.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Private equity funds value their holdings quarterly using manager-led appraisals, comparable multiples, and discounted cash flow models rather than continuous market prices. Because these marks update slowly and lag public market shifts, reported private equity returns exhibit artificial smoothing—a phenomenon often called volatility laundering. This smoothing understates true economic risk, lowers measured correlation and beta relative to public equities, and inflates risk-adjusted metrics like Sharpe ratios, making private funds appear safer and more diversifying than their underlying leveraged businesses actually are.

Valuation discretion also skews return comparisons. Interim performance measures such as internal rates of return (IRR) and public market equivalent (PME) ratios rely heavily on unrealized net asset values, where stale pricing and managerial judgment can delay write-downs during downturns or flatter marks around fundraising, distorting timing relative to daily-priced public benchmarks. Consequently, institutional investors can misjudge alpha, underestimate true leverage and equity sensitivity, and misallocate capital when comparing mark-to-model private assets directly against mark-to-market public equities.
